item.title: Re: Greenlight request- Frozen Corpse and Nervous System
item.content:encoded:
ok. I am willing to GREENLIGHT this, but I am going to warn you that this doesn't seem to be a strong narrative.

A few nitpicks:

+ show block
– hide block

This:

This is part of the reason I intend to add the audio file, not just for the story/narrative, but for the sound effects the skip makes, (cracking, sloshing, banging, skittering, etc.) and the scientist's reactions, which I think will add to the discomfort factor (I know audio is what made SCP-682 so infamous, not that my intention is to mimic that article).

Does not address my concern below:

so just a gory description of this anomaly isn’t really story rich, or all that unique

Body horror is very common on the wiki (suggest you look at Sarkicism Hub) so even if the audio is gross and the description is gross… that's not a story. For example, have you seen any slasher horror movies? Impressive gory violence isn't exactly a story beat… its meant to shock

What I am saying is: DONT rely only on the body horror to make your article work. Do more than imply characterization, because without something to relate to… the reader will just think "gross" and maybe that'll work for some but just as likely it won't work for others.

The second addendum mentions that other researchers heard the whisper, describing it as an indiscriminate noise, and recommended further research in case it meant something (without mentioning what the whisper said, or that it was even a whisper).

If I am not mistaken, we (as the readers) will hear this whisper in the audiofile, yes? So if we can understand it, how would 2 separate researchers be unable to recognize speech?

The origin is implied in the description section. I mention the shrunken portions of the brain that control cognition, motor functions, memory, etc, without explicitly stating their function- it just says frontal lobe, parietal lobe, and hippocampus without explaining to the reader why that's significant; I don't intend to talk down to them.

To me, this would not imply that the fetus took the mother's brain. A fetus has a brain I think… or a protobrain like organ that is developing.

Essentially it's a downer ending as the skip can't get what it wants, despite its hardships. Because its still technically alive at the end, it's left open-ended, though. Do you think it should not be open-ended?

I think "open ended" can be good. This does not seem open-ended, it seems shallow of facts/plot. I think you need to expand this in terms of the narrative… why would the child do this? Why would this have happened at all? Why should the Foundation care at all?

item.title: Re: Greenlight request- Frozen Corpse and Nervous System
item.content:encoded:
+ show block
– hide block

What are the origins of this anomaly?

The implications I'm making are that the fetus developed a mutation that absorbed the mother's brain matter into itself, then caused the rest of its body to dissolve and sink into the legs. The nervous system in the legs pulls itself away from the top half.

What closure would you think would make sense?

The skip manages to use all its effort in the observation session to make it clear it wants to return to a family member (causing the top half to whisper), but can't manage to do it a second time, and its attempts are thus dismissed as too speculative for the researchers to take action on. So much time is spent on trying to recreate the circumstances to repeat the message it left in the recorded session that it ends up consuming too much of its own body and deflates, becoming sluggish and close to death. The lead scientist decides to freeze it indefinitely until a solid answer on whether the mutation can happen again is found, or if a way to regenerate the consumed tissue is discovered. Essentially it's a downer ending as the skip can't get what it wants, despite its hardships. Because its still technically alive at the end, it's left open-ended, though. Do you think it should not be open-ended?

And then how could you imply those things without maybe explicitly stating them?

The origin is implied in the description section. I mention the shrunken portions of the brain that control cognition, motor functions, memory, etc, without explicitly stating their function- it just says frontal lobe, parietal lobe, and hippocampus without explaining to the reader why that's significant; I don't intend to talk down to them. I mention that the bisecting tear is along the uterus and the pattern of the tear suggests that the woman was pulled apart rather than cut in half, but that there are no markings or scars to suggest that an outside force caused it, leading the reader to consider that something inside her caused the bisection (the fetus, which is listed as cryptically missing or nonexistent). I mention the DNA in the living neurons are a near match to the corpse, implying that it is not a foreign force taking over the legs, but either living remains of the fetus and/or the woman herself.

The conclusion is implied in the addenda. The first addendum is the audio file where the top half's whisper is heard, and the transcript where the whisper is excluded. This is called to the listener's attention beforehand when the scientist stops, claiming he thinks he saw an arm move, implying that there is life in the top half.

The second addendum mentions that other researchers heard the whisper, describing it as an indiscriminate noise, and recommended further research in case it meant something (without mentioning what the whisper said, or that it was even a whisper). The lead scientist recreates the situation several times in hopes that it will happen again and tests for living tissue in the throat and mouth but repeatedly finds nothing and eventually dismisses the whole argument that it made any significant sound. This hints to the reader that it may have spoken something, so they will listen to the audio file closely and try to decipher it on their own.

The third addendum simply mentions that it has consumed itself too much during its time outside the freezer and will be preserved cryogenically, rather than through conventional freezing.

Basically, I'm hoping to get the readers to piece the puzzle together on their own through both reading and listening, which I think would make a unique experience, but that's up to you if you agree.

so just a gory description of this anomaly isn’t really story rich, or all that unique

This is part of the reason I intend to add the audio file, not just for the story/narrative, but for the sound effects the skip makes, (cracking, sloshing, banging, skittering, etc.) and the scientist's reactions, which I think will add to the discomfort factor (I know audio is what made SCP-682 so infamous, not that my intention is to mimic that article). I also think that the observation session is what will give the skip some personality and characterization. Again, it's up to you if you think this is worth trying.

item.title: Re: Greenlight request- Frozen Corpse and Nervous System
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

I guess I'll explain what I can about the narrative; I wasn't going to, since this is only a brief initial pitch, but hopefully you'll find this to be interesting at least.

If you want greenlights on an idea, you have to pitch the whole idea and not just some of it.

My concern with the narrative here is that it feels…lacking in closure? It might work if you can get a reader to feel invested in the SCP and so it being frozen indefinitely ends up feeling like a huge sad moment; but it feels like it might be hard to land that in a way that works? Particularly since the freezing here is implied to be perfect (i.e., that they've circumvented the usual issues where ice shards form within a body and rupture the cells); and so in turn, there's an implication that even if they wait a really long time, they could still wake her up?

The other issue with doing a sad ending here is that it feels like it might be really hard to get a reader to emphasise with the legs here; like…it's not like they can really talk and be a character and so you're likely going to have to rely on characterising them via their actions and mannerisms.


I'm willing to greenlight this though because I don't think either thing here is a major issue, and I think it'll be easier to tell if it works via a draft y'know? This said: there's a possibility this might work best as a tale and I'd urge you to seriously consider that. It'd allow you to spend a lot more time in the researchers mind if this was like…a write up of that investigation happening and his reaction to stuff, than if like, he has to formally write it up in a SCP file, y'know?

item.title: Re: Greenlight request- Frozen Corpse and Nervous System
item.content:encoded:
I guess I'll explain what I can about the narrative; I wasn't going to, since this is only a brief initial pitch, but hopefully you'll find this to be interesting at least. Here's the plot summary:

+ show block
– hide block

I'm hoping that the reader will interpret that by the absence of fetal tissue in the enlarged uterus and the shrunken portions of the woman's brain that regulate cognitive functions, sensory input, movement, and memory, that the fetus mutated in a way that caused it to absorb the mother's brain functions and dissolve, sinking into the legs with only the nervous system surviving, which means that the nervous system is essentially a hive mind of the mother and fetus. The mother had been wandering as a result of her brain's degradation and died in the snow, being frozen for an indiscriminate amount of time so that it would be difficult to pinpoint when she died. When the corpse thawed, the legs and lower torso forcibly pulled itself away from the upper body, confused due to its overall lack of "brain power," but with enough sense of direction (likely due to the mutation, or perhaps from the mother's prior knowledge and memory) to know approximately where the nearest village is, but never finds its way there and is instead picked up by the foundation when villagers report seeing it in the distance. It returns to the top half of the corpse before being acquired. The information that helps the reader determine this is revealed in different segments in the description section.

The scientist's observation session, which he commentates for the audio file, involves the scientist explaining that in the last two sessions, it had tried to exit the lab, so for this one, he has evacuated and disinfected the halls to observe what the skip does when it's let out. It blindly but frantically crawls along walls, feeling each doorway before coming to the facility's north exit and being adamant about trying to move through the exit, likely because it can sense the air coming from the outside. After failing to open the door by kicking it, it quickly scurries back to the freezer unit it's kept in and huddles back against its top half, connecting with it like a puzzle piece. As the scientist ends the session and closes the freezer, he hesitates, thinking he saw the top half's arm move, but dismisses it as a trick of light from the leg twitching. As he closes it, a raspy voice whispering, "Need Dad," can be briefly heard as the door is closing (this is not included in the transcript, only the audio file). Since the entity is likely a hive mind, the reader is left to interpret that it is looking for a specific family member, either the baby's father or the mother's father, who probably lived in the village where it was found. The reader will hopefully interpret that the skip was able to transfer some of its neurons to the top half to briefly control the mouth and vocal cords, and when the skip was initially acquired in two pieces, it was probably attempting to do the same thing. So it longs for closure.

The scientist doesn't hear the voice coming from the top half and dismisses the session as only partly informative about what it can do. He keeps the skip frozen to preserve its lifespan until it can be determined if this was a single mutation or something contagious that can happen again. A second addendum reveals that some researchers who listened to the scientist's recording noticed the indiscriminate sound as he closed the door, but the scientist has failed in his attempts to recreate the circumstances that allowed the whisper to be heard. He dismisses it as a noise that he perhaps made involuntarily as he closed the freezer door, thus dooming the skip to be frozen indefinitely.

I hope this is enough to constitute a beginning, middle, and end for a narrative. If you don't agree or don't find it interesting, let me know.

item.title: Greenlight request- Frozen Corpse and Nervous System
item.content:encoded:
I moved and trimmed your thread summary, since it was taking up extra space in the main forum screen. Try to keep thread descriptions (the text in the little box under the thread title) and titles short so you don't crowd out other authors in the forum listing. ~Zyn

Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Horror (body horror)

Page Layout (Optional): Class, containment procedures, description, addenda (including a voiceover mp3 file with sound effects)

Elevator Pitch: Pregnant woman is found frozen in the arctic, torn in half, fetus missing. Top half of body is dead, lower half moves erratically on its own, possibly with a purpose or cognition.

Central Narrative: Corpse was found frozen in Yukon when villagers noticed a strange, unidentified creature moving erratically. Corpse's lower half is controlled by a series of live neurons that consume the bone and ligament tissue and shock the muscles into moving convulsively, allowing it to crawl. It will violently hyperextend its joints (bending knees backwards and such) and break its own bones to move.

+ show block
– hide block

The live neuron DNA matches the dead woman, whose brain is somewhat shrunken, or possibly her fetus. Lead scientist believes it's capable of navigation and is searching for something. During observation session, which is recorded as audio file, corpse's bottom half attempts to navigate the facility's halls and leave through the exit, which is locked, then scurries back to its top half in its freezer unit. As scientist closes the freezer door, listeners may hear the corpse vocalize its desire for its father, which is not written in transcript. Scientist does not hear it, dismissing it as his own involuntary vocalization. He regrets that the skip's lifespan is so short as a result of consuming its own flesh and progressively deflating in size, that they'll never know what it wants, so it must remain frozen to stay alive until the foundation finds a way to save it, find what it's looking for, or determine how it came to be.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Using body horror as a focus, of which I haven't seen much here, and a full story with open-ended conclusion that is coherent with beginning, middle, and end if the reader reads between the lines. Specifically, I'd like to include a voiceover file from the scientist's observation session with written transcript, recording the skittering and cracking noises the skip makes, with a subtle hint/easter egg for readers to listen for, revealing what it's capable of, and possibly answering the question of what it actually wants (this won't be included in the transcript, so that the reader is left to think and interpret it on their own).

Additional Notes: Please advise how to include the mp3 file with submission, as it's essential to the storytelling, thanks.


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn
